newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's new leaders preach political re-education.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's new leaders preach political re-education.

text.p: Zaire's new leaders, under pressure to form a broad-based transitional government, on Monday preached political re-education from peasant collectives upward before national elections could be held.

In a statement redolent with the rhetoric of 1960s anti-colonialism, a senior aide to self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila urged patience over an election date as Kabila's forces consolidated their hold over the capital.

In Johannesburg, South Africa's deputy president Thabo Mbeki said Kabila would announce a new government on Tuesday night for the huge nation he has renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo. Mbeki met Kabila in Lubumbashi on Sunday.
South Africa's President Nelson Mandela said in Zimbabwe that Kabila would enter Kinshasa on Tuesday.

Ousted Zaire president Mobutu Sese Seko meanwhile rested in Togo's capital Lome after leaving his jungle palace in his home region of Gbadolite on Zaire's northern border, a security source there said.
"We must reawaken the population politically. It is our first duty," Kabila aide Deogratias Bugera told a news conference in Kinshasa on Monday.
"The aim is to avoid the possibility in the future that any one man can confiscate power," he said, accusing Mobutu of plundering what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations.
Despite Kabila's Marxist beginnings, there was no evident intention of establishing a communist-style state, as Bugera preached a need for economic independence and free enterprise.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said the United Nations was ready to work with a new government but he added:
"We should not forget that apart from the alliance there have been other political opposition movements in Zaire and the other political movements will have to be brought in."
The sprawling capital regained some of its bustle on Monday, the first working day after the dramatic overthrow of Mobutu.

In a strong sign of confidence in Kabila, the Zaire currency more than doubled in value against the dollar. Moneychangers on Kinshasa's "Wall Street" posted the zaire at about 70,000 to the U.S. currency, against 185,000 to the dollar last week.
Traders said this had more to do with a desire to conform to rebel wishes than any sudden change in economic conditions.
A mixture of euphoria and bloodshed greeted Saturday's rebel takeover that swept aside 32 years of Mobutu rule.
The local Red Cross put the death toll at about 200, both looters shot by rebels and lynched Mobutu soldiers.
Witnesses reported scattered looting as well as pockets of resistance from diehard presidential guards on Monday.

Many city shops were open and traffic and people were out on the streets. Students chanted anti-Mobutu slogans in scattered demonstrations of support for Kabila and his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL).
The ferry crossing between Kinshasa and Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo across the river, remained blocked.
Newspapers appearing for the first time since Friday's climax to a seven-month rebel offensive toasted Kabila.
"Kabila - president of the Republic," headlined the independent daily Potentiel in a special edition.
It also fronted a file photo of Mobutu's last defence minister and army chief, General Mahele Bokungo Lieko, killed by loyalist troops after trying to strike a deal with Kabila.
"General Mahele spilled his blood to save the people of Kinshasa from carnage," the caption read.

Japan, a major importer of metals from Zaire, hinted it would recognise Kabila's government, following a similar move by South Africa and cautious endorsement by the United States and former colonial power Belgium.
Germany said on Monday it was ready to cooperate with Kabila and joined Western calls for a rapid transition to democracy.
